newsitem.title: FRANCE: Euro battle takes centre-stage in French campaign.
newsitem.headline: Euro battle takes centre-stage in French campaign.

text.p: A battle over the terms for a single European currency grabbed centre-stage on Wednesday in the French parliamentary election campaign, with international organisations fuelling both sides of the argument.

The opposition Socialist party underlined its conditions for supporting European economic and monetary union (EMU), while the ruling centre-right coalition tried to convince anxious voters that no new bout of austerity was needed to meet the criteria.
The first opinion poll taken since President Jacques Chirac called a snap election for May 25 and June 1 suggested the coalition would win comfortably with a sharply reduced majority.
But another survey found most voters expected to be hit by further austerity measures after the election.

Both camps found support for their case from abroad. The executive European Commission gave the government a boost by forecasting that France would meet the key criterion to qualify for EMU, holding the public deficit to three percent of gross domestic product both this year and next.

But the International Monetary Fund (IMF) gave credence to Socialist warnings of a fresh wave of austerity to come by saying France needed to take more measures to cut its deficit durably below three percent.
In another setback for Prime Minister Alain Juppe, the IMF forecast French unemployment would continue to rise to more than 13 percent by mid-1997 from a record 12.8 percent in March.
Socialist spokesman Francois Hollande said after party leaders met: "We want the single currency, but with conditions."

These were creating a "European government" as a political counterweight to an independent central bank; ensuring that Italy, Spain and Britain if it wishes join from the start; agreeing an EU pact for solidarity and growth to promote jobs; and ensuring the euro is not overvalued against the dollar.

Socialist economic spokesman Dominique Strauss-Kahn called into question strict adherence to the deficit limit, saying in an interview with Le Monde: "Even if it's clear public deficits cannot be allowed to slip, there is no point making an unjustified dogma out of the three percent criterion."
On the government side, Budget Minister Alain Lamassoure told Reuters there was absolutely no need for further fiscal tightening to achieve the three percent deficit target.
"For the first three months of 1997...we are even ahead of our deficit reduction objective. We are not at all worried about the execution of the 1997 budget," he said.

The Union for French Democracy, junior partner in the ruling coalition, said achieving the single currency on time on January 1, 1999, was "a fundamental, non-negotiable objective" and accused the Socialists of betraying their European principles.
The UDF platform also called for "the creation of a hard core of (EU) states which favour closer integration, led by France and Germany".
"The Socialists have to a great extent abandoned their European ideal as the price for Communist votes," UDF leader Francois Leotard told a news conference.

French financial markets were calmer after three days of election jitters. The franc, bonds and stocks were all stronger, partly on the first poll taken since Chirac dissolved parliament showing the centre-right would win.
The CSA institute survey suggested that the centre-right would win 332 of the 555 seats in metropolitan France to 222 for the combined left-wing opposition and one for the far-right National Front.
The coalition held 464 of the 577 seats in the outgoing assembly, including most of the 22 seats in overseas departments and territories which are not covered by opinion polls.
Chirac gave cabinet ministers' their election campaign marching orders, urging them to take a message of confidence and energy to voters while continuing to fulfil their duties.
In a gesture to coalition unity, Chirac had a reconciliation meeting with his bitter 1995 presidential rival, fellow Gaullist ex-prime minister Edouard Balladur.
Balladur's chief lieutenant, Nicolas Sarkozy, was also rehabilitated and made one of the campaign spokesmen.
